Hi Daniel —

Thanks for the clear list. Below I've provided explicit, technical answers and the pre-approved wording you can include in your RFP response. I've also attached NetworkTopology.png which shows our regional routing and peering topology.

1) RTO (Recovery Time Objective) — standard operating targets
- Hosted (Redwood API): control plane detection -> automated routing to fallback model shards + prefix cache reuse. Mean RTO (control-plane initiated failover): 3–8 minutes. Worst-case RTO (region-wide cloud provider outage requiring manual mitigation and cross-region VM provisioning): up to 90 minutes.
- Dedicated (reserved pools): default RTO depends on pool configuration: with warm standby in a second region, mean RTO 5–20 minutes; without standby (cold failover) expect 1–3 hours for provisioning and model warm-up. These are configurable in the Dedicated contract.

2) RPO (Recovery Point Objective) — data/state considerations
- Inference requests are stateless by design; request/response artifacts are not required to be replayed to continue serving.
- KV cache and prefix caches: asynchronous replication by default (near-real-time), typical observed replication lag < 5 minutes. For enterprise Dedicated customers, we offer synchronous replication mode for critical KV prefixes with RPO ~0–5 seconds for that namespace.
- Logs, telemetry, billing events: replicated to multi-region storage with retention policies; RPO for telemetry is 0–15 minutes depending on pipeline backpressure.

3) Multi-region failover design
- Default: active-primary / warm-standby secondary regions. We maintain pre-warmed model slices and periodic KV cache snapshotting to speed recovery.
- Enterprise option: active-active across two regions using consistent hashing and global traffic routing (Layer 7 LB + intelligent client affinity). This requires network peering and consistent model version pinning.
- Routing and state continuity: control plane updates routing table, edge LB (our regional CDN peering) begins directing traffic to secondary region; ephemeral session continuity is preserved by routing based on request fingerprint and by warming KV caches from snapshots and recent prefixes.

4) Expected failover times (typical metrics)
- Automated detection + control-plane re-route -> reachability to secondary region: 1–3 minutes.
- Traffic cutover + model load + cache warm-up (typical) -> 7–15 minutes to reach steady-state p50 latency.
- Full steady-state with warmed caches for heavy-tail prefixes -> up to 45 minutes p95 in worst-case without synchronous replication.

5) Testing cadence & evidence
- Scheduled DR drills: quarterly tabletop reviews + semi-annual live failovers for core-hosted tenants. Dedicated customers can opt into monthly or quarterly live failovers as part of their support package.
- Artifacts available on request: runbooks (Failover_Runbook_v1.docx), post-mortem summaries from previous drills, test snapshots, and a change-log. We can provide sanitized post-mortems that remove customer-identifying details.

6) Security and compliance overlap
- We retain signed attestations and test logs in a secure audit store (multi-region). SOC 2 artifacts show quarterly drill results and policy adherence.

Notes & caveats:
- Exact RTO/RPO specifics will map to the deployment model you choose (hosted vs dedicated) and whether you enable synchronous replication / active-active routing.
- Network route convergence times depend on your WAN/CDN policies if you're using an on-prem edge.
